message.content:
The main differences between a CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing; handles OS, applications, and complex logic. | Parallel processing for graphics rendering and data‑parallel workloads. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for low latency, high clock speed, and complex branching. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores designed for throughput and parallelism. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set architecture (CISC) with sophisticated control flow. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) style; many identical cores execute the same operation on different data. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large caches per core, deep memory hierarchy, strong single‑thread performance. | Smaller per‑core caches but massive shared memory bandwidth; often uses dedicated VRAM. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, decision making, I/O, OS kernel operations. | Tasks that can be split into many independent operations: graphics rasterization, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training. |
| **Performance metric** | FLOPS per core × clock speed × cache efficiency → good single‑thread performance. | Total FLOPS from many cores → excels at throughput for data‑parallel tasks. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core but higher overall power due to fewer cores. | High raw throughput but lower energy per FLOP for massively parallel workloads. |

In short, CPUs are great for diverse, sequential tasks with complex logic, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on thousands of data elements simultaneously.
